entities.name: Charles the Child
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Charles the Child (or the Young), born around 847 and dying on October 3, 866, was the King of Aquitaine from October 855 until his premature death. The third son of Charles the Bald, King of West Francia and later Holy Roman Emperor, Charles the Child's nominal reign was a strategic move by his father to assert control over the often rebellious sub-kingdom of Aquitaine, following a period of intense internal strife and Viking incursions. His brief tenure highlights the persistent challenges to Carolingian central authority and the complex dynastic politics that characterized the fragmentation of the Frankish Empire in the 9th century.

Crowned by his father at Limoges in October 855, Charles the Child's rule was largely symbolic due to his extreme youth. His father, Charles the Bald, maintained effective control over Aquitaine, often intervening directly in its administration and defense. This arrangement was intended to pacify the Aquitanian nobility, who frequently sought more autonomy or aligned with rival Carolingian claimants. Despite his title, Charles the Child faced no major rebellions or significant military campaigns under his direct leadership, as his father remained the primary architect of policy and defense for the region, particularly against the persistent Viking raids that plagued the Loire Valley and other coastal areas.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Charles the Child's brief, nominal rule as King of Aquitaine from 855-866 serves as a case study for the fragmentation of the Carolingian Empire and the struggles of central authority against regional autonomy, particularly in the wake of the Treaty of Verdun. His early death complicated dynastic succession and underscored the precariousness of delegated power.
